mcqs.question: In Flutter, how do you typically add padding around a Text widget?
options: Set a padding property directly on the Text widget itself
Wrap the Text widget in a separate Padding widget that takes it as a child
Apply a global CSS-like stylesheet to all Text widgets
Padding is handled automatically and cannot be customized per widget
mcqs.explanation: Flutter's composability model expresses layout concerns like padding as their own wrapping widgets rather than properties bolted onto every widget — you nest a Padding widget around the child that needs the effect. There's no global stylesheet mechanism and no automatic uncustomizable default.

mcqs.question: Why can't a StatelessWidget hold mutable data that survives across rebuilds, the way a StatefulWidget's State object can?
options: StatelessWidget is a class, and only structs can hold state in Dart
The widget itself is disposable and recreated on every rebuild, so anything stored on it directly would reset with it; State is a separate, longer-lived object
It technically can, but Flutter's linter forbids it as a style rule only
StatelessWidget only differs from StatefulWidget in naming, with no functional difference
mcqs.explanation: Since the widget configuration object itself is thrown away and recreated on rebuilds, mutable data needs to live somewhere that persists across that — which is exactly the separate State object StatefulWidget provides. This is a real structural constraint, not a linter-only convention, and the two widget types do differ functionally.

mcqs.question: A widget's build() method directly calls an API to fetch data and stores the result in a local variable used in the returned widget tree. What's the bug?
options: The API call refetches on every rebuild, including rebuilds triggered by unrelated state changes elsewhere in the tree
This is correct usage — build() is specifically designed for data fetching
The bug is a compile error, since build() cannot contain function calls
The API call only runs once per app launch regardless of how many times build() executes
mcqs.explanation: build() can be invoked far more often than intuition suggests — any ancestor rebuild can trigger it — so a fetch placed directly inside it reruns every time, not just when the relevant data actually changed. Side effects like network calls belong in initState() or an explicit user action handler, not build() itself, which is expected to be fast and pure.

mcqs.question: A team wants app-wide state management with strong compile-time safety and easy unit testing without needing a BuildContext to read state. Which option best fits that specific requirement?
options: setState
Provider
Riverpod
Any of the four options are functionally identical for this requirement
mcqs.explanation: Riverpod was specifically designed to address Provider's reliance on BuildContext and add compile-time safety, making it the closest fit for that exact combination of requirements. setState is scoped to one widget's local state, not app-wide, and the four options are not functionally identical — they trade off differently on boilerplate, testability, and structure.

mcqs.question: An async fetch is started while a widget is on screen, but the widget is popped from the navigation stack before the fetch completes. The completion code calls setState directly with no guard. What happens?
options: Nothing — Flutter automatically cancels any pending setState call for a disposed widget
The setState call silently succeeds but has no visible effect
The widget is automatically remounted to receive the update
setState throws, since there's no longer a valid State object to update after dispose() has run
mcqs.explanation: Calling setState after a widget's State has been disposed throws, because the framework has no valid element to rebuild — this is why the mounted check exists as a standard guard before touching state in an async callback. There's no automatic cancellation or remounting behavior.
